paragraphs: In the third year of Yuanxing, the spring wind in Jingkou still carried the chill of the river.

At night the men passed around a permit brought back from the northern bank. It bore a Qin official seal authorizing refugees with papers to make the crossing, and several soldiers born north of the river recognized the names of the bends written on it at a glance. One said that Jiankang still owed their wages, and he had lived this long only to discover that crossing a river meant entering another register of life and death. Another refused to accept it. He folded the permit and handed it back to Liu Yu. If the Beifu Army could not even keep its soldiers' families with it, he asked, who would hold up its banners in the future? Liu Yu put the paper into his sleeve without answering at once.

Before Liu Yu returned, Jiankang had already been renamed the capital of Chu. On the day Huan Xuan took the imperial throne, an attendant removed the ceremonial crown from Sima Dezong’s head; its strings of jade beads struck together so loudly that everyone in the hall could hear. The new emperor ordered years of unresolved prison cases reopened and abolished several offices that existed in name alone. The measures were hurried, but some people truly benefited. A palace craftsman received wages long withheld. A family imprisoned after being punished for repairing a bridge for a nobleman was released. Twice the streets of Jiankang had cheered when the new dynasty opened its granaries.

By the winter month, however, the Chu court had drawn up a new military pay register, and matters changed. The veterans from Jingzhou demanded rewards; the palace guards in Jiankang needed new armor; the aristocratic houses that had submitted brought stacks of unpaid claims. Huan Xuan also had to guard against the Beifu men still in Jingkou and Guangling. He sent officials to search the commanderies for hidden stores of grain, but much of what first reached his granaries was the rice tenant families had set aside for winter.

In Danyang an old woman ran after a requisitioned grain cart all the way to the city gate, only then recognizing that the soldier leading it had once served in the Jin army. She caught hold of the wagon shaft and asked the young man whether he had changed uniforms yet again. He did not dare look at her; he only urged the ox forward.

The report Huan Xuan received in the palace said that the military grain quota had been met in full. Someone advised easing taxes and labor service for a year to let the new dynasty catch its breath. He replied that clemency would come once the old army at Jingkou had been swept away. He had never trusted those commanders. Liu Laozhi had once brought an entire Beifu army into his allegiance, yet had kept his own troops and loyalties. Now Liu Laozhi was dead, but He Wuji, Liu Yi, Liu Yu, and others still commanded devotion. With the dynasty renamed, Jingkou could no longer be permitted to harbor an armed force that honored the old Jin banner and refused to lay down its weapons.

Three disbandment orders came in succession. The first abolished the old unit designations; the second summoned commanders to Jiankang; the third demanded the surrender of weapons and the registers of naval vessels. When a county clerk came to collect swords, an old Beifu soldier pointed to his hilt. “I paid for this sword with two mu of my own land. At what rate will the court buy it back?” The clerk could not answer, so he entered the man’s name in the register of disobedience.

Liu Yu had seen a way of taking an army apart at the Fei River. Under Fu Jian, Qin registers and military orders let the troops know who was responsible for grain and who could audit the accounts. Now Jingkou received a piece of paper from the Chu court demanding weapons, while no one would even verify how many months' pay was overdue. Returning from the north, Liu Yu often passed villages where people secretly left rice beneath tree roots, covering it with bundles of wet grass for fear of being denounced for aiding rebels. He left money in payment, only to find the coins returned untouched the following day. The villagers would rather lose their rice than leave behind a receipt that might be used as evidence against them.

The five-day agreement at the Fei was over. Liu Yu led his men out of the waterways on schedule, leaving only a small detachment to guard the boats as the rest returned to Jingkou in successive groups. By the time he was ready to rise in arms, he could assemble barely two thousand men that night. Some had checked grain with him at Xinting the year before; others were veterans who had never taken off their armor after the rebellion of Sun En.

Someone asked why he did not call all the Beifu garrisons together. Liu Yu said Jingkou was not yet in their hands; no one would risk the parents, wives, and children of an entire prefecture on his word. A few thousand willing to follow were enough to decide where they would march tonight.

He Wuji sent him a secret letter bearing only the drawing of a broken bow. They met in a ruined riverside temple, where wooden memorial tablets for soldiers fallen under the former dynasty still stood against the wall. He Wuji said Huan Xiu, who held Jingkou, had three thousand troops. Fewer than half were men he had brought from Jingzhou; most of the others had been enrolled using the old Beifu registers. Someone had promised to unlock the eastern gate, but word had come that morning that the inside agent had been discovered. Fearing exposure, Liu Yi wanted to withdraw to Suan Mountain and wait for replies from elsewhere.

Liu Yu burned the letter and did not answer immediately. Water dripped from the eaves onto a broken stele. He stared at the old saber at He Wuji’s waist and recalled how, when Liu Laozhi and Huan Xuan were testing each other in Jiankang, the Beifu Army had not even known which road it was meant to hold. In the end both commander and soldiers had become counters in other men’s hands.
“If Jingkou changes its guards again tomorrow,” Liu Yu said, “the people willing to open the gate for us today will truly be dead.”

At midnight the insurgents hid among reeds south of Jingkou. The smell of wine from the battlements mingled with the wet scent of the grass. Some defenders were making jokes about old Beifu soldiers, saying that since Liu Jinu had bargained with the Qin ruler, he must have come back south as a Qin lackey. He Wuji gripped his sword, his face livid, and stopped only when Liu Yu raised a hand.

No agreed signal fire rose within the gate. Only the short horn call of the watch change sounded from the walls. Liu Yu told the others to remain in the reeds and went up the levee with two veterans. The first arrows came while he was still more than a hundred paces from the gate. One sank into the mud beside him; another tore the sleeve of an old soldier. Liu Yu raised his scabbard and called the gate captain by name in the accent of Jingkou.

The captain had once been a junior clerk under Liu Laozhi. Now wearing Chu armor, he recognized the voice but dared not acknowledge it. He asked whose edict Liu Yu carried. Liu Yu asked in return whether the register of unpaid wages in the city had been handed over to Huan Xiu. The captain faltered. Among the dozens of former Beifu men stationed on the wall, many had received only two months' wages the year before. Now Huan Xiu intended to enter the debts afresh on the principle that “the new dynasty is not liable for old debts.” Complaints erupted immediately. The captain ordered the archers to fire, but an old soldier beside him pressed a hand against the back of a bow.

“Your families live in Jingkou.” Looking up at the dark figures on the wall, Liu Yu did not raise his voice. “So does mine. Open the gates tonight, and we will inspect the grain stores first. We will write down who owes each old debt. If we cannot find the answer tomorrow, I will come back to this gate and listen while you curse me.”

The captain shouted that he was corrupting the troops. Then a gate guard came running up from below, crying that townspeople had surrounded the winch behind the gate and Chu patrolmen had slashed two of them. The captain wheeled around. Liu Yu signaled toward the reeds. He Wuji’s men lit their torches and rushed forward.

The winch creaked inside, but the gate opened only halfway. Soldiers struggled over the crossbeam on either side. As Liu Yu reached the entrance, a section of timber nearly crashed onto his shoulder. He and the two veterans held the gate leaf steady while He Wuji led the vanguard through the gap. Close fighting broke out inside the passage, sword blades striking the stone walls, the echoes waking the houses nearby.

Not until the fourth watch did a different banner rise over Jingkou. The former gate captain was captured wounded, and Liu Yu ordered a physician to stop his bleeding first. He Wuji argued that the man had ordered the archers to fire and deserved beheading at the least. Liu Yu asked how many guards had actually loosed a second arrow on his orders. He Wuji did not know. So Liu Yu had the captain and the gate guards detained separately for questioning the next day. Men who had just fought their way into a city most wanted to settle the night’s debts in one satisfying reckoning. At precisely that moment Liu Yu ordered every unit back to its street post and forbade anyone from storming into civilian homes to take revenge.

In the morning the government granary was unsealed. Inside were bolts of silk and military pay that Huan Xiu had not managed to remove. On seeing the accounts, Liu Yi proposed distributing rewards immediately to secure the allegiance of the insurgents. Liu Yu took him to the granary entrance. Along the wall sat a row of civilian grain porters; some bore whip marks on their legs from Chu soldiers pursuing grain sacks the day before. Their wages were recorded in the same general account as the money and silk, but always ranked behind the soldiers' rewards.
“Pay the arrears according to the register first,” Liu Yu said. “The porters' wages too. Seal what remains in the granary.”
“We have risked our lives to rise,” Liu Yi said under his breath. “If you use the money to settle old debts before rewarding the men, they may not obey you.”
“They have fought beside me, and they have gone hungry beside me. They know whose money is being repaid today.”

Liu Yi left, his face set. That afternoon a dispatch arrived from Guangling: Meng Chang and the others had joined the uprising, seized the government stores and ferryboats, and were ready to unite with Jingkou. Liu Yu ordered the messenger to report the quantities of grain and the number of boats again. Meng Chang’s reply was exact, omitting not even two old vessels that leaked. He Wuji laughed. “That man keeps better accounts than the accountants at court.” Liu Yu placed the bamboo dispatch at the head of the council table and ordered boats prepared. At last, one command from Huan Xuan had failed to lock both gateways, Jingkou and Guangling.

On the night before the army marched, an old woman brought half a sack of steamed cakes. She said her two sons had served in the old Beifu Army, and neither had come home. She did not want the military office to repay her. She wanted someone to record beside which river or bridge their bodies had been buried. Liu Yu summoned a scribe and had him write down both sons' names, unit numbers, and last recorded dispatches. The woman studied the page and asked: if he, too, died out there this time, who would keep the records for soldiers' families? Liu Yu could not answer. He merely folded the page into her palm and told her to keep it.

The Beifu Army moved west along the river, gaining followers day by day. Some counties opened their gates at its approach; others sent messengers to both sides. The magistrate of Qu’a knelt beside the road in Jin official robes newly put back on. The old Beifu commanders wanted him killed: he had once welcomed Huan Xuan into the city and imprisoned three elderly officials who refused to use the Chu reign title.

Liu Yu first ordered the prison opened, then inspected the granary. There was little grain in store, but a quantity of requisitioned millet not yet handed over remained under seal. The magistrate argued that had he refused the Chu orders, Huan’s army would have entered and searched the town for grain. Liu Yu asked how the three old officials had been punished. One had a broken wrist; the other two had only been confined. Ashen-faced, the magistrate acknowledged each offense in turn.

Liu Yu ordered him to oversee grain transport temporarily, compensate and tend the injured official, and submit to a separate investigation by an inspector. Whether he should be dismissed was left for judgment after Jiankang was recovered. He Wuji was unhappy. With such leniency, he said, every opportunistic official along their march could escape punishment by offering a granary. Liu Yu pointed to the thousand or more mouths waiting to be fed south of the city. Killing one magistrate today took only one stroke of a sword. If there was no grain tomorrow, was he supposed to cut down all thousand as well? He Wuji said nothing more, but as they left the county he urged the scribes to bring every page of the testimony. Not a single sheet was to be lost.

As they reached a market town west of Dantu, the first grave case under their military law arose. Du Qian, a valiant commander in the vanguard who had helped seize the gate at Jingkou, still carried two arrow scars on his shoulder. Hearing that a wealthy household had supplied the Chu army with grain, he led men to raid the estate, then seized the cattle of several neighboring tenant families as well. An old man tried to keep hold of his own thin ox. A blade fell at the threshold, and blood ran down a gutter into the stone mortar used for pounding grain.

When Liu Yu arrived, the old man was still breathing. A child knelt beside him, clutching the ox rope in both hands. Du Qian produced an account book containing real quantities of grain provided to Chu, and argued that requisitioning supplies in wartime had always allowed exceptional measures. Liu Yu asked exactly what debt the wounded old man owed. Du Qian said he tilled the rich household’s land and therefore shared its guilt. The child pointed at the ox behind Du Qian and sobbed for him to give back his grandfather. Anger flashed across Du Qian’s face, and he kicked away the bloodstained rope.
That kick shamed the soldiers standing nearby more than any argument over grain.

Liu Yu ordered Du Qian arrested, sent a physician to help the old man, and sealed all the confiscated property. He Wuji hurried over, invoked Du Qian’s service in the taking of Jingkou, and asked that he be flogged and stripped of command but allowed to live and atone. Liu Yu waited until the physician emerged and said, “He cannot be saved.” Only then did he order a military judge to take testimony under the regulations enacted at Jingkou. Du Qian admitted drawing the blade, but denied that taking the ox was a crime. His comrades had risked their lives clearing the road, he said; surely they deserved some reward. When the judge read out the offense of “a commander unlawfully seizing civilian property and killing an unarmed person,” Du Qian stood erect and did not plead for mercy.

Several former subordinates knelt to intercede before the execution. Liu Yu refused. By the time the blade fell, dusk was gathering. Even the men cooking gruel in camp dared not speak loudly. Some cursed Liu Yu for making a sacrifice of a meritorious officer; others said that saving the commander on a battlefield might no longer buy a man his life.

The next day the army indeed ran short of grain. People in the town shut their doors and refused to sell so much as a dou of millet. Liu Yu forbade anyone to threaten them. Not until afternoon did the village headman bring three carts of grain, insisting each cart was a loan, not a gift. Liu Yu had the quartermaster write debt certificates with a separate value for each household, then pressed his own validating mark onto them. The headman took the papers and, on his way out, still walked around the newly washed bloodstain outside the military office.

The news reached Jiankang while Huan Xuan was discussing the ceremonial carriages of his new dynasty. One minister said Du Qian had been a seasoned officer and that Liu Yu’s act would surely cost him his soldiers' loyalty. But Huan Xuan was staring at a report of commanderies and counties opening their granaries along the Beifu route. Men at war sometimes feared the swords of their enemies, and sometimes feared even more that their own people might come to believe another army would repay the grain it took. Huan Xuan ordered Wu Fuzhi not to wait for reinforcements but to occupy Luoluo Bridge and destroy Liu Yu. He sent Huan Qian with more troops to intercept the advance. The Beifu Army must not be allowed closer to Jiankang.

Rain had swollen the water at Luoluo Bridge. Wu Fuzhi placed crossbowmen south of it and had the small boats nearby dismantled or carried away. After examining the terrain, Liu Yu chose not to storm the bridge in the expected fashion. First he sent He Wuji and picked men to ford a shallow reach upstream. By night the water stood above their chests, and the soldiers linked themselves with ropes. Several swallowed water and nearly dragged their entire group under. He Wuji hauled at the man before him while cutting the weeds wrapped about his feet. By the time they felt their way to the southern bank, their hands and feet were numb with cold and dawn was showing along the sky.

Liu Yu attacked the bridge head-on. In the first charge the bamboo shields were burned through. In the second, a rotten bridge plank gave way beneath their feet, throwing several men into the water. When the Beifu Army charged a third time, Wu Fuzhi’s crossbowmen still held the bridge under a murderous screen. An arrow struck Liu Yu’s lamellar cuirass, and a notch was hacked from his sword.

At the height of the southern army’s drumbeat, He Wuji cut in behind the bridge. Battle cries from fewer than five hundred men rose in the rear of the Chu forces. Wu Fuzhi mistook them for an enemy that had seized his whole line of retreat and hastily ordered his rear ranks to turn. With no one left to replenish the forward crossbows, a gap opened for an instant. Liu Yu rushed to the middle of the bridge, and the men behind him poured over the wet planking. Wu Fuzhi was killed and the Chu formation broke.

The Beifu Army, too, had paid dearly. Some of the bodies floating out from under the bridge still had ropes tied around them, linking them to men of their unit. He Wuji knelt on the bank to undo the knot binding one fallen soldier. His frozen fingers would scarcely obey him. Looking up, he saw Liu Yu giving a clerk the unit numbers of those killed. He Wuji suddenly held out the piece of rope he had just freed and asked that every man who had crossed the water be entered by name—not only the enemy commanders they had slain.

Two days later the Beifu Army came within sight of Fuzhou Mountain near Jiankang. When the Chu garrison heard of Wu Fuzhi’s death, fresh rumors spread day and night. Some claimed Liu Yu had fifty thousand men; others that he had borrowed Qin cavalry. Huan Xuan ordered the palace carriages prepared and officials ready to escort the Jin emperor and imperial clan west. He still had his old Jingzhou troops and the granaries of Jiangling, and believed that what he lost in the east he could one day regain. He considered burning several granaries in Jiankang, but in the end did not issue the edict. The officer responsible for setting the fires waited all night. At dawn all he heard was the urgent drum calling men to board the boats.

When the Vermilion Bird Gate opened, the first to emerge were defenders who had stripped off their Chu armor. Liu Yu did not let his troops charge into the palace precinct. First he sealed the granaries and secured several city quarters vulnerable to fire. Several dignitaries from great families came out dressed in Jin robes, insisting they had served Chu only as a pretense. Liu Yu ordered them to carry all household registers and grain accounts left in their offices to the Secretariat; he was in no hurry to hear declarations of loyalty.

At the Secretariat, he found an old grain requisition register from Wu Commandery. The same villages had been taxed by the Jin court, then by the army sent to suppress Sun En, then by Huan Xuan’s men. The last line read: “Able-bodied men dead or scattered; no one left to answer for the arrears.” Liu Muzhi brought him the figures for the city’s stores, while He Wuji urged that the Jin banner be raised at once. Liu Yu agreed, but forbade a great celebratory banquet. The Jin emperor was still on Huan Xuan’s boat; Jiangling still held a strong army; and the streets were full of unpaid soldiers, starving men, and people stripped of their possessions.
He Wuji asked who would preside over the provisional government. Liu Yu glanced at him. “You will. The old Beifu soldiers know Liu Laozhi’s nephew, and the court nobles know you as well.”
“And you?”
“Inspect the granaries. Receive surrenders. Have someone bring me the names of the men who died at the bridge.”

At dusk, several tattered Jin flags were found in an old palace storehouse. Attendants stitched their edges and hung them over the Vermilion Bird Gate in the wind that had not yet dried after the rain. Some laughed, some wept, and some stood at the roadside watching nothing but the military grain carts. Liu Yu rode beneath the wall, raised his eyes once, and returned to the Secretariat. The Jin emperor had not yet truly been brought back, and Huan Xuan had not been captured. The fate of this city was settled, but the course of the south still lay buried in those scattered ledgers.
On the night the Beifu Army returned, the lamps at the Secretariat burned longer than those in the great hall of the palace.
